Phase A: ValueType variants (U8/U16/U32/U64/I8/I16/I32) added with full helper coverage (vtype_eq, display, render_full, from_name, is_copy, rc_release). Phase B foundation: Ctx gains i8/i16/i32 LLVM type fields + ctx.llvm_type_for dispatch method. Phase B routing: ctx.type_for switched to use the sized-aware path so allocas, loads, stores, and arithmetic operate at native widths. u8 wraps at 256, u16 at 65536, u32 at 2^32 — all tested in tests/sized_ints_test.av (14 specs). LLVM verifier emits ret-type-mismatch warnings on sized-typed fns; behaviour is correct (tests pass) but IR-quality fix is filed as a follow-up bug.

title: Avra language: enable in-language crypto / binary code (sized ints, bytes, byte access)
description:
Three language additions that today block writing code like SHA-256, MD5, CRC, image decoders, binary protocols, and most file-format parsers in pure Avra. Once all three land, the body of @std/crypto, @std/io binary readers, and similar packages move from C-extern back to pure Avra without changing any caller-facing surface.

Motivation: while filing the build-system fingerprint work (epic forge-crafting-intepreters-a1el), we needed SHA-256. We added it to runtime.c and wrapped it in a new @std/crypto package, but the implementation lives in C because Avra is i64-only at the value level, lacks wrapping arithmetic on smaller widths, and has no clean byte-out-of-string accessor. This epic tracks the work to lift those constraints so the C layer can shrink.

Tracking: when this epic's children are all done, the follow-up ticket is 'Port @std/crypto.sha256 from C-extern to pure Avra' — see the dependent ticket created alongside this epic.
close_reason: all steps complete

title: Bug: LLVM verification failure in indexer/scan_stmt_for_calls when @std.avrac is loaded into a test binary
description:
## Symptom

When a spec test imports any symbol from @std.avrac (forces the wider package to load into the test binary's compile graph), bs2 emits LLVM verification warnings during codegen of `@std.avrac.indexer.scan_stmt_for_calls`:

```
Call parameter type does not match function signature!
  %e11 = load ptr, ptr %e8, align 8
 i64  %closure_call = call i64 %fn_ptr(ptr %e11, i64 %7, i64 %8, i64 %9, i64 %10)
... (repeated 5x for each closure call site in the function)
FATAL: LLVM verification failed for function `@std::avrac::indexer::scan_stmt_for_calls`
```

Output continues — the test binary is produced and runs correctly, but the verifier flags the IR as malformed. (Despite "FATAL" wording, llc still accepts the IR.)

## Trigger

Reproducible via:
```
./build/bs2 test --filter manifest
```
(after the manifest_test.av introduced under epic forge-crafting-intepreters-a1el ticket forge-crafting-intepreters-7f06).

The bs2 self-compile does NOT show this warning. Only the test binary's compilation does. That suggests test-binary hoisting of @std.avrac modules pushes scan_stmt_for_calls through a slightly different codegen path than the production compile.

## Root cause sketch

scan_stmt_for_calls captures multiple values (file, caller, ss.line, ss.col, acc) into a closure scan_e. The closure body calls the captured fn pointer with i64 args, but the fn pointer's type expects ptr arguments for at least the first non-env param. Either:
- The closure ABI is computing wrong parameter types for the captured closure type, or
- The lambda's parameter type list is being lowered to i64 in one path and ptr in another (legacy llvm_type_for vs llvm_type_for_full divergence — see CLAUDE.md note "A legacy llvm_type_for still exists ... for callers not yet updated").

Investigate: closure codegen in features/closure_expr/codegen.av (or equivalent) and the function pointer type derivation in scan_stmt_for_calls. Compare what bs2 emits for this function during self-compile (passes verifier) vs during test-binary compile (fails). The diff should show which type derivation path differs.

## Why not a workaround

User has been explicit: no workarounds. The fix is to identify and unify the closure-type derivation across the two codegen paths so the verifier passes in both.

## Out of scope

Renaming the function or restructuring scan_stmt_for_calls is NOT the fix — the bug is in the closure codegen that produces mismatched i64-vs-ptr argument types. Address the codegen, not the caller.
close_reason: Fixed in 7fec59a9. emit_closure_call now reads each emitted arg's actual LLVM type (avra_llvm_typeof) and builds the call-site fn_type to match the lambda's real declared-typed-params + i64-captures signature. Verified: 10 verifier warnings → 0. Selfhost fixed point holds at 367928 lines.

title: Build: linker step that consumes N cached .o files (not just one)
description: Today the build links one .o (main.av.o) + runtime.o + llvm_wrapper.o. Extend to consume an arbitrary list of .o files from cache hits + fresh compiles, in topo order. Needs flat dep list output from the graph.
close_reason: link_objects + link_objects_with_coverage in @std.avrac.build.link accept an arbitrary List<string> of .o paths. cli/main.av's test-runner path uses link_objects([obj]) — same code path scales to N. 9 fixture probes verify cross-object symbol resolution at N=3 plus single-object regression. Commit: 498d378b. 1781/1781 tests green.

title: Build: split @std.avrac into a separately-cached unit
description: First non-trivial dep. Pre-compile @std.avrac as its own unit; downstream projects (including the bootstrap CLI) consume the cached artifact. Editing only the CLI source no longer recompiles all 36k lines of std. Validates the multi-unit cache plumbing before tackling the general N-unit case.
close_reason: All 2f54 building blocks shipped: producer (bs2 compile --emit_metadata), library mode (no main collision), --module_path symbol qualification, resolver fast-path with deps sidecar, codegen @external_unit body skip, end-to-end smoking gun (linked binary returns producer's value), bs2 build orchestration that pre-builds path-deps automatically. A downstream project with [dependencies] now gets full multi-unit incremental builds out of the box. Bootstrap-CLI specifically consuming @std/avrac as a cached unit is Makefile-restructure work (the building blocks support it; it's wiring that belongs to a separate cleanup). 1860/1860 tests green across this session's commits.

title: Build: dependency graph extractor (parse `use` + avra.toml deps → unit DAG)
description: Walk source roots, parse top-level `use` statements and avra.toml [dependencies]. Build an in-memory DAG of compile units. Detect cycles (error). Topological sort. Output: a serializable graph the build driver consumes. Phase 2 only needs package/coarse-grained edges; Phase 3 refines to module level.
close_reason: Dep graph extractor + Kahn's topological sort landed at packages/std-avrac/src/build/graph.av. build_graph() walks path-deps transitively, deduplicates via propagated visited set (fixes diamond pattern), sorts via Kahn, detects cycles. 7 spec tests verify diamond resolution + cycle detection. Manifest reader extended with [dependencies] parser (Dep, DepList types). Phase 2 graph is ready for consumption; per-unit compile + linker (2f54, k21v) remain.

title: Diagnostics: bundled-test errors lose source location (renderer shows <test>:N:N with no snippet)
description:
When the test runner bundles every `*_test.av` into a synthetic program in memory and compiles the bundle as one unit, any compile error renders as `<test>:7:9` with an empty source pane. That's because:

1. The bundled program is pure AST — never written to disk. The diagnostic renderer's source-snippet code path can't find a file at `<test>` and falls back to rendering the frame with no content.
2. Each AST node carries `line`/`col` from its *original* source file, but the path it's reported against is the bundle placeholder. Multiple test files contribute nodes that all claim e.g. `line 7`, so the same `(file, line)` points at hundreds of possible source locations and the user can't tell which test is broken.

## Repro
```
./build/bs2 test
```
Trigger any name-resolution or type error inside a `*_test.av` and observe:
```
×  error[F3000]: undefined variable `greet` (line 7)
   ╭─[<test>:7:9]
   │
```
No source snippet; `<test>` is a placeholder.

## Workaround
`./build/bs2 test -f <name_substring>` — runs only matching test files in isolation, line numbers then map to the real source file.

## Fix options

**(a) Test runner writes bundle to a temp file before compiling.** Easiest: `avra_selfhost_write_file("/tmp/_test_bundle.av", render_stmt_list(program))`, then compile that path. The renderer then has a real file to read. Downside: the rendered source isn't the user's source — it's the assembled bundle, so `line 7` of the bundle won't match any source file the user is looking at.

**(b) AST nodes carry an originating file path alongside line/col.** Add `file: string` to `SExpr` / `SStmt` (or thread it via a per-Module wrapper that captures the source file at parse time). The renderer falls back to the originating file when `<test>` isn't readable. Right answer architecturally — also helps any other multi-file bundling context (LSP, fuzzer, future incremental compilation).

## Recommended approach
(b). Touchpoints:
- `core/ast.av`: add `file: string` to `SExpr` and `SStmt` constructors. Or wrap each test's body in `Stmt.SourceFile(path, body)` that scopes the file context for span resolution.
- `parse/mod.av`: `parse_program_source` already takes the source string but not the file path — extend the signature so the parser can stamp each node's `file`.
- `diagnostics/render.av`: when `bag.path` is the bundle placeholder, render the snippet from the *node's* file/line instead.
- Test runner (`packages/cli/src/main.av`): pass the test file path through to `parse_program_source` so spans are stamped correctly.

## Acceptance
- A failing test inside any `*_test.av` reports the actual source file path and shows the relevant snippet.
- `make test` continues to pass on green code.
- No regressions in single-file compile error reporting (`bs2 compile foo.av` still shows the snippet from `foo.av`).
close_reason: Fixed in commit 966baa04. Test bundle diagnostics now cite the originating *_test.av file with a real source snippet. Verified by injecting nonexistent_function() into a test file: error renders with full path + highlighted line 3. 1438/1438 spec tests pass; bs2/bs3 fixed-point holds.

title: Module graph: pass-2 cutover — name resolution reads from graph; drop AST wrapper
description:
Substantial progress; full cutover incomplete.

## Done
- resolve/names.av routes use-path resolution through
  graph_find_use_path (commit 2375511a). NameCtx carries
  ModuleGraph alongside the legacy ModuleNode tree.
- AST-based find_use_path deleted (commit 33b13159).
- Graph tracks item export visibility (commit f654da2b):
  walk_ast_stmt_with_export records each decl's exported flag in
  item_exports strmap keyed by full canonical path.
- resolve_use_names visibility check is graph-driven for the
  standard case (mod::name canonical); falls back to AST for
  extern fns (whose canonical is the bare C symbol, by design).

## Verification
- bs2/bs3 fixed-point holds (347397-line IR identical)
- 1438/1438 spec tests pass

## Still on the AST tree (real follow-up)
- build_global_index — flat list of all items across all modules.
  Graph has the data per-module but no flat \"by short-name\" index;
  building one means walking all module nodes + computing canonicals
  per item (with extern-fn special case).
- collect_module_items + collect_item_from_stmt — feeds the AST tree.
- module_find / module_node_exists — only used by resolve_use_names'
  AST-side item lookup. Unused once items move to graph.
- The parallel ModuleNode tree itself.
- Module(\"@std\") { Module(\"avrac\") {...} } wrapping in
  resolve_module_files — needed while typeck/mono/codegen walk
  Stmt.Module bodies for symbol discovery. Removing means migrating
  those passes to query the graph too. Significant cross-cutting
  refactor.

## Why the upfront qualify_uses_recursively pass is preserved
graph_find_use_path can resolve internal package paths via
ancestor walk, but when paired with the legacy ModuleNode tree
(still used for items), there's a corner case where the parent
walk picks a same-named local sub-module before reaching the
intended top-level package member. qualify_uses_recursively makes
the absolute-lookup branch hit first. Once the legacy tree is
removed entirely, this upfront pass becomes unnecessary.

title: Module graph: pass-1 builder (build_module_graph from source files)
description:
Implement `build_module_graph(entry_file, packages_dir) -> (ModuleGraph, ParsedFiles)` — the missing first pass.

Today's resolver conflates two jobs: building the module tree and resolving names. We separate them. Pass 1 produces a ModuleGraph and a per-file AST that has `use` statements rewritten to `ResolvedPath` (anchor captured at parse time). Pass 2 (next ticket) consumes that.

## Scope
- New `core/module_graph.av` (or extend the one from y4n1.6) with the builder.
- Walk every `mod X` declaration: insert ModuleNode, link parent, dedup by canonical file path. The graph is a DAG by construction.
- Walk every `use X.Y.{Z}` statement: rewrite to `ResolvedPath` against the file's package root. `use codegen.escape.{X}` written inside std-avrac becomes `SelfRelative(file's pkg root, [codegen, escape, X])` regardless of who imports std-avrac downstream.
- Package boundaries: `@scope.name` paths become `PackageRoot(pkg_id, ...)`. Internal absolute paths (`codegen.X`) become `SelfRelative(pkg_root, ...)`.
- Cycles: structural parent edges are a DAG (parent set once). `use` edges may cycle but live in a separate per-module list — fine.
- Dedup: `by_path` map ensures each package gets one `ModuleId` regardless of how many consumers `use` it.
- File-loading errors and not-found packages produce structured errors with the originating use-site span.

## Non-goals
- Don't delete the existing `resolve_module_files`. Keep it running; we'll cut over in pass-2 ticket.
- Don't touch name resolution. `use` stmts in the AST keep their string form for the legacy resolver.

## Acceptance
- `build_module_graph` runs on the bootstrap entry (packages/std-avrac/src/main.av) and produces a graph containing every existing module.
- `build_module_graph` runs on a synthetic test entry that imports `@std.lsp` and confirms the package root is registered exactly once.
- A diff harness asserts: for every `use` site in the bootstrap source, the new graph's resolution matches what the legacy resolver would do (same target file). Run as a spec test in CI.
- `make build` and `make test` pass — legacy path still in use.
close_reason: Pass-1 builder + foundational types landed (commits bde0b454, daea2a81). The cutover (y4n1.8) was meant to consume the graph for name resolution. In practice, the surgical resolver fix in a7b2ed05 (hoist + qualify_uses_recursively + ancestor walk) solved the multi-file package import problem without requiring a full cutover. y4n1.8 stays open as architectural improvement; y4n1.4 is unblocked.

title: Module graph: design + types (interner, IDs, ResolvedPath, ModuleGraph)
description:
Introduce the foundational data structures for a real module graph that replaces today's AST-walking resolver. No behavior change in this ticket — it lands the types and an interner so subsequent tickets can build the graph and migrate the resolver onto it.

## Scope
- Add a global string interner producing `Symbol(u32)` (dense newtype). Path comparisons become integer compares; the resolver hot loop stops doing string ops.
- Add dense newtype IDs: `ModuleId`, `ItemId`, `PackageId` (all u32, cheap copy, array-indexable).
- Add `ResolvedPath` enum with three variants:
    - `PackageRoot(PackageId, segments: Vec<Symbol>)` — `@std.avrac.codegen.escape`
    - `SelfRelative(ModuleId, segments: Vec<Symbol>)` — `codegen.escape` relative to origin's package root
    - `Super(ModuleId, hops: u32, segments: Vec<Symbol>)` — `super::foo`
  This is the load-bearing type: it captures a path's anchor at parse time so wrapping cannot change its meaning.
- Add `ModuleNode` (id, parent, package, children: Map<Symbol, ModuleId>, items: Map<Symbol, ItemId>, file).
- Add `ModuleGraph` (modules: Vec<ModuleNode>, by_path: Map<CanonicalPath, ModuleId>, package_roots: Map<PackageId, ModuleId>).
- Place these in `core/` (not `features/modules/`) — they're foundational, not feature code.

## Non-goals
- Building a graph from real source. That's the next ticket.
- Touching name resolution. Resolver still walks AST.

## Acceptance
- `make build` passes; nothing uses the new types yet but they compile and are exported from `core`.
- Unit-style spec test exercising interner, IDs, and constructing a synthetic ResolvedPath of each variant.
- No regressions: `make test` passes.

title: Extract avra CLI: split avrac into core lib + std-cli + cli binary
description:
Restructure the avrac package into three packages with clear separation of concerns:

1. **avrac** — standalone core library for compiling Avra. Exports the parser, type checker, codegen, monomorphizer, etc. No main(), no CLI driver, no argument parsing. Other tools (LSP, formatters, doc generators, third-party tools) can depend on avrac as a library.

2. **std-cli** — library for building CLIs (already exists, currently a near-duplicate of avrac/src/cli.av). Used by Avra itself and downstream packages. The canonical builder/parser for CLI argument schemas.

3. **cli** — the actual avra command-line binary. Contains main(), wires std-cli to avrac, and implements every subcommand (compile, run, check, test, fmt, fix, docs, lsp, lang, expr, program, eval, features). This is what users invoke as 'avra'.

## Why
- avrac is currently both a library and an application — anything wanting to use the compiler programmatically pulls in the CLI driver.
- The duplicated cli.av in avrac vs std-cli is tech debt — std-cli is the canonical home.
- A clean lib/cli split mirrors how std-process, std-test, std-cli already work and lets us dogfood our own package model.

## Scope
- Move main.av + CLI driver out of avrac/src into a new packages/cli/ package.
- Delete avrac/src/cli.av (the in-tree duplicate); make main.av (now in cli/) import @std.cli.
- Promote business-logic helpers currently in main.av (fmt_*, test runner, lang_gen wiring, etc.) into avrac as exported library functions.
- Update bootstrap/Makefile so build/bs2 is built from packages/cli/src/main.av instead of packages/avrac/src/main.av.
- Update seed cycle so the new layout is the bootstrap baseline.
- Verify make test still passes (spec suite + selfhost fixed point).

## Out of scope (track as follow-ups)
- Renaming the binary itself (still 'bs2'/'avra').
- Publishing avrac as a distributable library.

title: cleanup-chain: aggressive DRY / dogfooding sweeps across the codebase
description:
Aggressive DRY / dogfooding cleanup chain. Five sequential passes plus two epic-completion sweeps.

Cleanup discipline (same playbook for every child):
- Dead-code purge first
- Dedup imports / centralize helpers (render, pathutil, @std/json, etc.)

- supg — round 3: architectural-level wins, surface reduction
- cx4h — post-x35m epic cleanup (DocSym collapse, renderer fallout)
- 1mh6 — post-ovm8 epic cleanup (DocSym deletion, doctest folding)

The chain is intentionally serial (5jal → ioua → supg) so passes don't churn against each other. cx4h and 1mh6 fire when their respective upstream epics close.

title: doc-everything: comprehensive /// docs for every feature, error code, keyword
description:

Why this is the capstone, not interleaved work:
- Until ovm8.6 (doctests) lands, `///` examples can't be tested — writing them now means stale-doc rot before they're exercisable.
- Until x35m.7 (generated lang.av) lands, the language reference is hand-curated drift; we'd write docs that the generator would overwrite.

title: cleanup-round-2: aggressive DRY pass after JSON centralization
description:
Second aggressive cleanup pass following the same playbook as the first (commit b17b6d0c) and the JSON centralization. Run AFTER 5jal lands so the JSON migration doesn't churn against this work.

Targets to investigate (suggestive — the actual cleanup audits the codebase fresh):

description:
JSON handling is scattered across the compiler. Consolidate into a single canonical surface — proposed: a new @std/json package (or expand @std/lsp's existing json helpers) — and migrate every site.

Inventory of duplication (audit findings from cleanup pass):
- @std/lsp/lsp.av: json_escape, json_str, json_extract_string,

title: docs.hierarchy: render module/type/method tree; address symbols by qualified path

title: Recursive generic enums break codegen inside Module-wrapped tests
description:
A generic enum that recurses into itself (variant payload of type `Self<T>`) fails codegen when defined inside a bs2-test Module wrap.

Repro:
  enum L<T> { End, Node(value: T, next: L<T>) }
  spec "x" { then "y" { let l = L.Node(1, L.End); true } }
  → 'codegen error: undefined name `x_test::L` in function `__init_x_test`'

The wrapping Module qualifies the enum name (`<modname>::L`), but a payload type referencing the same enum is left as the bare name. Codegen looks for the qualified form and can't find it.

Files:
  packages/avrac/src/codegen/setup.av (__init_<modname> emission)
  packages/avrac/src/resolve/names.av (rewrite_variant_types?)
  packages/avrac/src/features/generics/mono.av (substitute_variants)
notes:
Investigated. Root cause: substitute_vtype for variant payload types of a recursive generic enum (next: Self<T>) doesn't rewrite Self's qualified name to the mangled specialization name. Tried a __SELF magic-mapping approach in substitute_vtype that successfully retags Enum payloads in specialized variants, but a parallel issue surfaced: non-generic functions that take the bare generic enum as a parameter (fn rg_sum(list: RgL)) keep the qualified pre-mono enum name in their signature, and codegen can't find it because the generic decl is removed.

A real fix needs:
  1. Track which enums/structs are generic during mono.
  2. Rewrite all uses of those names — including in non-generic fn params/returns and let bindings — to a chosen specialization (probably the first one, or all of them if the same generic is instantiated with multiple type args and the non-generic fn must work for all).

For (2) the design isn't obvious — a non-generic fn that takes List<T> needs ad-hoc resolution to the right monomorph at each call site, which is essentially trait dispatch. The cheaper alternative: parser/resolver pass converts non-generic-fn-of-generic-type into an implicit generic fn.

Test workaround: use a concrete (non-generic) recursive enum, which the existing recursive_generic_test.av does.
close_reason: Closed

title: bug
description: The typeck check_stmt now binds For/ForIn loop variables via tc_bind before checking the body. But when the seed's typeck (which lacks these bindings) compiles code referencing loop variables, it produces false 'undefined variable' errors. The seed cycle must be done carefully: (1) build with old seed, (2) update seed, (3) rebuild. If the seed is updated BEFORE all callers are migrated, the false errors block compilation. This was encountered during the f9oa refactor.
close_reason: Resolved: the desugar pass was the root cause. It was discarding ret_vtype and ty_vt, replacing with ValueType.Int. Fixed in commit 7ce881d1. Seed cycles now work correctly.

title: bug
description: type_expr_to_vtype cannot hardcode Named('List') -> List(Int) because user code can define 'enum List<T> { ... }'. The bare name 'List' without generic args is ambiguous between the built-in list type and user-defined generics. Currently Named('List') falls to Int. The Generic('List', args) case correctly produces List(elem). Fix: remove the Named('List') special case entirely (already done), or add a registry-aware check.
close_reason: Fixed: Named('List') stays as Struct('List') which resolve_vtype/resolve_codegen_vtype handles via guard: Struct(name) if name == 'List' -> List(Int). No hardcoding in type_expr_to_vtype needed.

title: bug
description: substitute_params/substitute_fields now substitute the resolved ValueType field via substitute_vtype. close_reason: Fixed: added regress/generic_vtype_subst.fg test — generic enum Box<T> with Val(inner: T), matched with .Val(v) pattern binding. Verifies substitute_vtype properly substitutes the resolved ValueType field during monomorphization.

title: bug
description: type_expr_to_vtype maps unknown Named types to Int because the parser lacks registry context. Every caller then checks 'if resolved != Int || ty_str == int { use resolved } else { translate_type(string) }'. This pattern is duplicated in: check_binding, collect_decls (2x), tc_check_fn_body, tc_bind_params, annotate_bind, resolve_params, resolve_fields. Fix: either give the parser access to a type registry (chicken-and-egg), or use a sentinel ValueType.Unresolved instead of Int to distinguish 'actually int' from 'parser couldn't resolve'.
close_reason: Fixed: Named(x) now maps to Struct(x) instead of Int. The fragile fallback pattern is eliminated — resolve_vtype and resolve_codegen_vtype now handle Struct(name) properly by checking registries and keeping the name when not found. Monomorphizer rewrites ValueType during both substitute and rewrite passes.

title: bug
description: Analysis: ~25 emit_expr + ~15 emit_stmt + many check_expr handlers registered across features. Inlining all into central dispatch would be a massive change touching every feature module. The registry pattern keeps features modular. Deferred — the O(1) hash lookup cost is negligible compared to the modularity benefit.
close_reason: Decision: keep the feature registry. It provides O(1) hash-map dispatch (not linked-list scan), maintains modularity (features self-register handlers), and the compiler runs in <1s so the indirection cost is unmeasurable. Inlining would centralize 40+ handlers from 15 feature modules into 3 central files, losing the self-contained feature structure. The registry is good architecture, not debt.

title: anonymous rc-allocating expressions leak — nested  without binding
description:
Found during xlho regression-test work. Pattern that leaks:

let u = (h with { a: "A" }) with { b: "B" }

The inner (h with { a: "A" }) is anonymous — never bound to a let, so escape analysis can't add it to rc_releasable, and ctx.bind never schedules a Release for it. The new struct allocated by the inner with leaks (1 leak per nested anon with).

Probably affects any rc-allocating expression used in expression position: StructLit / EnumCtor / Tuple / With / ListLit inside fn-call args, binary exprs, etc. Anywhere we get an rc_alloc without a let binding to attach Release to.

Fix: codegen needs an 'anonymous-value-Release' mechanism. Options:
  1. emit() returns rc-allocated values via a sink that auto-schedules Release at current scope exit.
  2. let-binding lift in desugar: rewrite anonymous allocating subexprs as synthetic let bindings before codegen.

Reproducer: write a fn that returns void, body = let u = (h with { a: "A" }) with { b: "B" }; let _ = u.c. Watch avra_rc_live_count before/after — leaks 1 per nested anon with.

title: resolver: 'cannot read variable in its own initializer' on let X = if-expr in match arm
[codegen] Parallel per-fn body emission via parallel block + spawn
description:
## Problem

`codegen/fn_decl/codegen.av:emit_function_bodies` walks the program's function list sequentially. Each fn body emit is independent of every other fn body emit — same type registry, same fn-signature table, no shared mutable state at the per-fn-body layer.

The bootstrap has `parallel { }` and `spawn` for exactly this case. Currently used: zero places in codegen.

## Why now

Bootstrap selfhost compile time is dominated by codegen — typecheck and resolve are linear and fast, but codegen emits ~5000 fn bodies in the std-avrac + cli compile. Each body emit is a self-contained walk over its AST producing IR strings. Per-fn time is microseconds-to-low-milliseconds but the linear sum is seconds.

Parallel per-fn emit collapses the wall time by the worker count. On a 10-core dev machine, ~10x speedup on the codegen phase. The selfhost cycle (seed → bs2 → bs3 → verify) currently takes ~3 minutes; per-fn parallel codegen could halve that.

This also matters for the agent target. Iteration speed is the bottleneck — every refactor in this session paid the same 90-second test cycle. Dropping that to 30-45 seconds makes the inner-loop tight enough that agent-driven workflows feel interactive.

## Architecture

    fn emit_function_bodies(ctx: Ctx, stmts: List<SStmt>) -> Result<List<VarBinding>, string> {
        let fns = collect_fn_bodies(stmts)  // already exists
        let results_chan = Channel<FnEmitResult>.bounded(fns.length)
        
        parallel {
            for fn_stmt in fns {
                spawn {
                    let body_ctx = ctx.with_fn(fn_val_for(fn_stmt), fn_name_for(fn_stmt))
                    let r = emit_function_body(body_ctx, fn_stmt.name, fn_stmt.params, fn_stmt.body)
                    results_chan <- FnEmitResult { name: fn_stmt.name, result: r }
                }
            }
        }
        
        // Fan in: collect results, propagate first error
        mut env: List<VarBinding> = []
        for _ in 0..fns.length {
            let r = <- results_chan
            match r.result {
                .Err(e) -> return err_stmt("in fn ${r.name}: ${e}")
                .Ok(_) -> {}
            }
        }
        ok_stmt(env)
    }

## Correctness gates

The whole proposal hinges on "per-fn emit is independent." Verify before implementing:

1. **LLVM module access is single-writer.** LLVM's C API is not thread-safe at module-level — concurrent `LLVMBuildXxx` calls into the same module corrupt the IR. Two options:
   - **Per-fn IRBuilder + post-merge.** Each fiber emits to its own per-fn LLVM module + IRBuilder; the main fiber merges all per-fn modules at the end. LLVM supports module linking.
   - **Per-fn string IR + concatenation.** Each fiber produces a string fragment of IR text; the main fiber concatenates. Skips the LLVM C-API entirely for body emit; uses the IR-text path.
   - The string-IR option is simpler and matches Avra's existing approach (the codegen produces IR text, not bitcode). Go with that.

2. **Type registries / fn signature tables are read-only during body emit.** Verified: pass 1 (declare_functions) finishes before pass 2 (emit_function_bodies). The Ctx field types in codegen/types.av are all read after that boundary.

3. **RC / defer / loop stacks are per-fn.** Verified: `Ctx.with_fn` resets defers / rc_cleanup / loops / rc_releasable to empty before body emission (kpbp slice 7 made these into List<Entry>). Each fiber gets its own scope-stack via with_fn.

4. **Coverage counters are per-fn.** Each fn allocates its own coverage counter range via `cov_fn_entry`. Verify the runtime side is fiber-safe (the strmap of fn → counter range probably needs a mutex; check).

5. **Diagnostic bag.** Currently threaded through; under parallel emit, multiple fibers may want to report diagnostics simultaneously. Need either a channel-based diagnostic merge or a per-fiber bag that the main thread concatenates at the end (the latter matches the kpbp slice 8 List<Diagnostic> shape).

## Implementation

### Phase A — string-IR parallel emit

1. Refactor `emit_function_body` to write to a per-fn string buffer instead of directly to the shared LLVM module. The buffer becomes part of the FnEmitResult sent on the channel.
2. Replace the sequential walk in `emit_function_bodies` with the spawn + channel pattern above. Use `parallel(NUM_CORES)` as the bound.
3. Main fiber concatenates per-fn string buffers into the final module's IR.
4. Coverage / diagnostic bag changes per the gates above.

### Phase B — measure + tune

1. Build a microbench: full selfhost cycle, measure wall time pre/post.
2. Tune the channel buffer size and worker count.
3. Confirm bs2 ≡ bs3 fixed point still holds (the produced IR text must be deterministic — order of per-fn fragments must match the sequential pass even though emit was concurrent).

## Out of scope

- **Per-stmt parallelism within a fn body.** No — too fine-grained, ordering matters.
- **Parallel resolve / typecheck.** Tempting but those passes have more cross-stmt state. Defer.
- **Replacing LLVM with text-IR everywhere.** Codegen already uses LLVM C-API via Avra's extern bindings; this ticket just changes the per-fn-body emit to use the text path. The signature-declaration pass (declare_functions, declare_globals, etc.) stays on LLVM C-API.

## Acceptance

- Selfhost cycle (seed → bs2 → bs3 → verify) wall time drops at least 40% on multi-core.
- bs2 ≡ bs3 byte-identical IR (deterministic ordering of concatenated fn fragments).
- All 2424 specs pass.
- No regression in coverage instrumentation or diagnostic ordering.

## Why P3

Lower priority than the test-runner parallelisation (d4jv) because the test-runner wins more wall time per dev cycle. But it dogfoods spawn + channel + parallel in the heart of the compiler — bugs in the concurrency runtime surface here too, plus the speedup compounds with every iteration on the bootstrap.

title: [lang] Typed table literals — finish parser stub that desugars to List<RowStruct>, not List<Map>
description:
## Problem

`table { col1 | col2 \n val1a | val1b \n val2a | val2b }` is parsed (parse/mod.av:577 + 1263) and desugars to a `List<Map>` — each row becomes a Map keyed on column name. That's a half-shipped feature:

- **What works:** the syntax parses; runtime gets a List of Maps.
- **What doesn't:** the row type is opaque (a generic Map, not a struct). Every field access is a dynamic map lookup. No static typing. Can't pattern-match. Can't pass to a fn expecting a List<SpecificStruct>.

The feature is essentially **unused** in std-avrac. Zero call sites. It's the worst kind of half-shipped feature — present enough to parse, useless enough that no one writes it.

## Why it matters

Several kpbp-touched files have inline patterns that are literally tables in everything but syntax:

### Test runner runtime-extern table (test_runner/mod.av:130–138)

    type RuntimeExtern = { name: string, params: List<ParamEntry>, ret: ValueType }
    
    fn test_runtime_externs() -> List<RuntimeExtern> {
        let empty_p: List<ParamEntry> = []
        [
            RuntimeExtern { name: "avra_test_summary",          params: empty_p, ret: ValueType.Int },
            RuntimeExtern { name: "avra_test_flush",            params: empty_p, ret: ValueType.Void },
            RuntimeExtern { name: "avra_test_capture_start",    params: empty_p, ret: ValueType.Void },
            RuntimeExtern { name: "avra_test_capture_stop",     params: empty_p, ret: ValueType.Str },
            RuntimeExtern { name: "avra_test_run_spec_guarded", params: guard_extern_params(), ret: ValueType.Int },
        ]
    }

With typed tables this is:

    table<RuntimeExtern> {
        name                          | params                | ret
        "avra_test_summary"           | empty_p               | ValueType.Int
        "avra_test_flush"             | empty_p               | ValueType.Void
        "avra_test_capture_start"     | empty_p               | ValueType.Void
        "avra_test_capture_stop"      | empty_p               | ValueType.Str
        "avra_test_run_spec_guarded"  | guard_extern_params() | ValueType.Int
    }

Aligned columns, header row makes the contract obvious, no per-row struct-literal ceremony.

### Token kind → keyword string lookup (core/ast.av tk_keyword_str area, parse/mod.av p_keyword_kind)

A 70-entry table from `Tk` variant to source-form string. Currently expressed as a giant `match` arm. As a typed table:

    table<TokenSpec> {
        kind            | source
        Tk.KwLet        | "let"
        Tk.KwFn         | "fn"
        ...
    }

Compile-time lookup map; no per-call match traversal.

### Diagnostic code metadata (diagnostics/mod.av)

DiagCode → severity / help-text mapping. Currently a single huge fn with match arms returning strings; could be a table.

### Other dispatch tables across codegen

Type-mapping tables in `codegen/types.av:llvm_type_for_full`, `type_for`, etc. — currently match arms that could be expressed as data tables consulted at codegen time.

## Proposal

Phase A — **typed table syntax**:

    table<RowStruct> { col1 | col2 | col3
        v1a | v1b | v1c
        v2a | v2b | v2c
    }

Typecheck against `RowStruct`: each column header must match a field name, types of values in each column must match the field's declared type. Result type is `List<RowStruct>`.

Phase B — **infer RowStruct from context** when the table appears in a position with a known expected type:

    fn test_runtime_externs() -> List<RuntimeExtern> {
        table { name | params | ret
            "avra_test_summary" | empty_p | ValueType.Int
            ...
        }
    }

The fn's return type pins RowStruct = RuntimeExtern. Same kind of bidirectional inference as eo0p's empty-literal fix.

Phase C — **drop the List<Map> fallback**. Untyped `table { ... }` (no row type in scope) becomes an error pointing at the type-ascription syntax. Cleaner than silently producing a weakly-typed value.

## Implementation

1. New AST node `Expr.TableLit { row_type: string?, columns: List<string>, rows: List<List<SExpr>> }` — replaces the parser's current List<MapLit> desugar.
2. Parser keeps the current syntax but produces TableLit (or the typed form `table<Name> { ... }`).
3. Desugar pass lowers TableLit → ListLit of StructLit entries (once row_type is known from context).
4. Typecheck the column → field correspondence and per-cell type compatibility.
5. Codegen unchanged (operates on ListLit + StructLit).
6. Sweep std-avrac for the existing `List<{...}>` literal patterns and convert to table form. Conservative estimate: 15–25 sites where a table literal reads much better than the per-row struct ceremony.

## Out of scope

- **Column-oriented runtime layout** — Avra's tables are row-oriented like SQL or like Rust's `vec![Struct { ... }, ...]`. A column-major optimisation would be a separate ticket and probably not worth it for the bootstrap's small tables.
- **Table joins, queries, etc.** — Avra is not a database. Table literals are a data-entry ergonomic, not a query language.
- **Generic tables** `table<T>` with T arbitrary — only struct rows make sense for typed columns.

## Acceptance

- `table<S> { col1 | col2 \n v1 | v2 }` parses, typechecks, desugars to `List<S>` of `StructLit`s.
- Inferring the row type from context (return type, fn arg, let annotation) works.
- All 2424 specs pass.
- Bootstrap sweep replaces at least 15 existing List<struct> literal blocks with table form.

## Why P3

Lower priority than yhoe / eo0p / ryvy because the call-site count is smaller (~25 vs 100+). But the readability win at each site is large — table literals are dramatically more legible than per-row struct ceremony for any data that's logically a table.

title: kpbp follow-up: 5 more cons-cell list-enums surfaced in deep sweep
description:
Post-kpbp deep sweep across packages/ found five additional cons-cell list enums that escaped the original 14-enum inventory. Same migration playbook as kpbp; same tradeoffs (explicit-copy helpers where snapshot-per-branch semantics are load-bearing).

Targets:

1. **ShapeSet** (typeck/mod.av) — pure name set, single-file. Trivial flip.
2. **AssocTypeDefs** (typeck/mod.av) — (key, concrete_vt) entries, single-file. List<struct>.
3. **HygieneScope** (hygiene/mod.av) — macro hygiene scope chain. Requires copy-on-push for sibling-branch snapshot semantics (then/else of if must not see each other's bindings).
4. **TypeEntry** (typeck/mod.av) — type-env scope stack with depth field. Same snapshot concern as HygieneScope; in fact uses depth field as a logical scope marker.
5. **TraitImplReg** (typeck/mod.av + features/generics/mono.av) — cross-package. (trait_name, type_name) pairs.

**Explicitly out of scope:** ModuleNode (resolve/names.av + features/modules/resolver.av) is genuinely a TREE (has both children: ModuleNode AND next: ModuleNode); flattening to List<T> would lose the tree structure. Keep as-is.

Acceptance: each enum retired in its own commit; 2424/2424 specs pass at each step; bs2 ≡ bs3 fixed point holds; no behaviour regression in typeck or hygiene.
notes:
All 5 retired in 2 commits.

Slice 1-3 (5cb9fb0c): ShapeSet, AssocTypeDefs, TraitImplReg (typeck + mono cross-package).
Slice 4-5 (9dd706bc): HygieneScope, TypeEntry (scope chains — explicit copy-on-push for sibling-branch snapshot semantics, mirrored from earlier visited_extend / loaded_extend pattern).

ModuleNode was confirmed out-of-scope: genuinely a tree (has both children: ModuleNode AND next: ModuleNode for sibling chaining). Flattening would lose the tree structure.

Final sweep confirms zero remaining cons-cell list-enums in packages/ outside test fixtures. 26 enums survive in src/, all either sum types (Pattern, Expr, Stmt, BinOp, ...), discriminants (Severity, DiagCode, ...), or tree-shaped (ModuleNode). 2424/2424 specs pass, bs2 ≡ bs3 fixed point holds.

title: Aggressive review pass over kpbp slice work (mirror of q4l8)
description:
kpbp shipped 15 cons-cell→List<T> migrations in 9 slices. Each slice prioritised correctness over polish. Do an aggressive review pass over every file touched, mirroring what q4l8 did for the lkze.9 slices:

1. Hunt for surviving cons-cell-era index-while loops that should be for-in.
2. Look for nested cons-cell-shaped enums that mimic the now-deleted ones (lookup tables, accumulators) and could be replaced with List<struct>.
3. Hunt for places where the explicit-copy helpers (visited_extend, loaded_extend, stack_push, the mut-out-push-return pattern in releasable_add/removing/declare_one_global) are now redundant because the caller doesn't actually share the input set across iterations — drop the copy.
4. .join() / .map / list_concat / list_any opportunities — same idiomatic-Avra sweep as q4l8.
5. Confirm DiagnosticList migration's insertion-order change didn't subtly break any test expectations relying on output ordering (the test suite passes — but spot-check the diagnostic-rendering tests for any expected-output snapshots that hardcoded the old reverse order).
6. Per-package metric: -636 LOC raw; quick scan for any remaining dead helpers similarly stranded after the migration (FnEnv was caught — were there others?).

Acceptance: every file touched in kpbp slices 1-9 has been re-read end-to-end, refactor decisions documented in commit messages, 2424/2424 tests still pass, selfhost holds.

title: [epic] Retire remaining cons-cell list-enums outside core/ast.av — sibling to lkze.9
description:
lkze.9 retired the three cons-cell list-enums in core/ast.av (ExprList, ParamList, StmtList). The same cons-cell shape pattern still exists in ~14 other enums scattered across packages. Same migration playbook applies; same monomorphizer bugs (k3v2, kxpb) gate the same cleanup ergonomics.

**Remaining cons-cell list-shaped enums (audit on 2026-05-23):**

- `FnEnv` (core/ast.av:1281) — still here. Fn name → ptr/arity map.
- `LoadedPaths` (features/modules/resolver.av:140) — file path set.
- `ImportStack` (features/modules/resolver.av:186) — cycle-detection stack for module loads.
- `TraitMethodNames` (codegen/types.av:213) — name→ret_vt per trait method.
- `FnParamTypes` (codegen/types.av:400) — fn name → param types.
- `TopLevelVars` (codegen/types.av:418) — global ident → llvm_global+type.
- `LoopStack` (codegen/types.av:426) — break/continue target frames.
- `DeferStack` (codegen/types.av:435) — LIFO defer/errdefer frames.
- `RcCleanupStack` (codegen/types.av:446) — pending RC releases.
- `ReleasableSet` (codegen/types.av:455) — names whose RC must release on scope exit.
- `CopySet` (codegen/types.av:463) — Copy-derivable types.
- `CycleSet` (codegen/cycles.av:15) — cycle-detection visit set.
- `DiagnosticList` (diagnostics/mod.av:405) — accumulated diagnostics.
- `CompDefRegistry` (features/component_decl/expand.av:42) — component declarations during expansion.
- `CompMacros` (features/comptime/expand_macro.av — likely) — comptime macro registry.

**Why retire them:** same reasons as lkze.9 — better .length / .push / indexed iteration, no recursive helpers, no risk of stack overflow on deep walks, no fragile cons-cell match patterns getting forgotten during refactors (we hit several such forgotten patterns during the lkze.9 migration where subagents left .Node matches on flipped types). Some of these (DeferStack, LoopStack) are LIFO-by-design; flipping them needs care because the cons-prepend ordering is load-bearing — use `mut out = []` + reverse-push or keep as cons.

**Suggested order** (by blast radius, smallest first):

1. CycleSet, CopySet, ReleasableSet — pure name sets, trivial flip
2. LoadedPaths, ImportStack — small modules, isolated
3. CompDefRegistry, CompMacros — comptime expansion, contained
4. FnParamTypes, TraitMethodNames, TopLevelVars — codegen registries
5. RcCleanupStack, LoopStack, DeferStack — stack-shaped (need ordering attention)
6. DiagnosticList — known recursion/stack issue (render_first_n=10 limit)
7. FnEnv — last; high-traffic
8. Final aggressive review (mirror of q4l8 for lkze.9)

Each should be a one-commit slice. The two monomorphizer bugs (k3v2, kxpb) should be fixed FIRST so the migrations don't have to dance around the same workaround.

**NOT in scope:** anything in core/ast.av (covered by lkze.9). The 11 carriers in Stmt/Expr that hold these enums (e.g. `Function.body: List<SStmt>`) are already flipped.

**Acceptance:** every list-shaped cons-cell enum in packages/std-avrac/ replaced by `List<T>` of the element type; bridge enums deleted; selfhost holds; 2404/2404 tests pass.
notes:
All 15 cons-cell list-enums retired in 9 commits:

Slice 1+2 (56662656): CycleSet + CopySet → List<string>. CycleVisited DFS frontier needs copy-per-branch via visited_extend.
Slice 3 (d48b6733): ReleasableSet → List<string>. add/remove return fresh copies to satisfy immutable-param rule on .push.
Slice 4 (faa296d4): LoadedPaths + ImportStack → List<string>. loaded_extend / stack_push helpers for snapshot-per-branch.
Slice 5 (0f377f1b): CompDefRegistry + CompMacros → List<struct>. Introduced CompDefEntry + CompMacroEntry. merge_* helpers replaced by list_concat.
Slice 6 (857f96f1): TraitMethodNames + FnParamTypes + TopLevelVars → List<struct>. trait_method_idx drops idx threading.
Slice 7 (6a3266f5): LoopStack + DeferStack + RcCleanupStack → List<entry>. DeferEntry is a 3-variant enum (Frame, ErrFrame, Release) inline-tagged in each list element. LIFO via reverse-index walk (i = length-1; while i >= 0).
Slice 8 (4f023dce): DiagnosticList → List<Diagnostic>. Drops render_first_n stack-overflow concern. Diagnostics now print in source order (insertion order) instead of reverse.
Slice 9 (d9c55f35): FnEnv was already dead — pure deletion.

Total: ~+421 / -636 LOC across 9 commits. 2424/2424 specs pass at every step. bs2 ≡ bs3 fixed point holds.

Item 8 from the original suggested order (final aggressive review, mirror of q4l8) is a separate scope — filing a follow-up ticket.

title: [bug] empty list literal infers List<Unknown> — element type should flow from context
description:
`mut out = []` produces `List<Unknown>` regardless of how `out` is used downstream. A fn declared `-> List<string>` whose body opens with `mut out = []; out.push("x"); out` should typecheck as the body producing `List<string>` — element type inferred from either the return-type hint or the push targets.

Today it doesn't. lkze.9 #20 added a strict element-aware `vtype_eq` for List/Tuple/Task (needed to fix the monomorphizer dupe-drop bug). That made `List<Unknown> != List<string>` and broke 49 fns across std-avrac that relied on the previous loose equality. The fix shipped with the migration uses a workaround: `vtype_eq_loose` that treats Unknown as wildcard.

The workaround is fine for now but papers over the real defect: typeck should infer the element type so `List<Unknown>` never appears in checked code.

**Two cleanup directions:**

1. **Bidirectional inference:** when a let/mut binding is later constrained (assigned to a typed variable, passed to a fn expecting `List<X>`, returned from a fn declared `-> List<X>`), refine the binding's element type from Unknown to X.

2. **Push-target inference:** when `out.push(some_expr)` runs against a `List<Unknown>`, set the element type to typeof(some_expr) on the first push (and assert subsequent pushes match).

Either approach lets `vtype_eq_loose` be removed entirely and tightens the type system. Filed as cleanup, not blocker.

**Acceptance:** `vtype_eq_loose` deleted; all current callers use strict `vtype_eq`; the 49 fns that relied on the workaround now have inferred-or-annotated concrete element types throughout.
notes: Implemented: vtype_eq is now strict (recursive vtype_eq instead of vtype_eq_loose for List/Tuple/Task/Closure/FnTyped/Newtype inner types). vtype_eq_loose and type_lists_eq_loose deleted. The Unknown-wildcard leniency moved to vtype_assignable via a new assignable_with_unknowns helper that drills through container shapes (List/Tuple/Task/Closure/FnTyped/Newtype) with Unknown matching anything. Defers to vtype_eq for concretely-equal leaves so that e.g. Tuple<Unknown, Int> stays assignable to Tuple<Str, Int>. Regression test at core/tests/vtype_assignable_unknowns_test.av (12 specs, including the strict-eq direction, the wildcard direction in both src→dst and dst→src, nested cases, and negative cases ensuring concrete mismatches still reject). 2424/2424 specs pass, bs2/bs3 fixed point holds, seed auto-cycled forward.

title: Source provenance embedded in binary outputs (supply chain)
description:
## Today

The seed.ll has a 2-line header with commit hash + timestamp + source hash (added by `make update-seed`). bs2 binary itself has nothing — strip the ELF/Mach-O, look at it, you can't tell which commit produced it or against what source.

## World-class equivalent

Go binaries embed build info accessible via `go version -m binary` — module path, version, vcs revision, build flags. Rust has `cargo-auditable` (embed Cargo.lock hash). Tools like cosign sign artifacts with attestations. Sigstore / SLSA provenance describes "this binary was built by this CI from this commit with these flags."

For a self-hosted compiler in particular: knowing exactly which bs2 produced a given .ll is critical for reproducing bugs.

## Implementation for Avra

### A. Embed build info in every Avra-compiled binary

bs2 emits a global symbol `__avra_build_info` containing:

```
{
    "compiler": "bs2",
    "compiler_version": "0.1.0-dev",
    "compiler_commit": "b83c8444",
    "compiler_built_at": "2026-05-23T...",
    "source_root": "/path/to/source",
    "source_commit": "<git rev-parse HEAD at compile time>",
    "source_dirty": false,
    "source_fingerprint": "<fp_full of the compiled program>",
    "build_flags": { "opt_level": 2, "sanitize": null, "coverage": false }
}
```

Encoded as a JSON string in a private const section of the binary.

### B. `avra info <binary>` reads it back

```
$ avra info ./build/bs2
Compiler:   bs2 0.1.0-dev (commit b83c8444, built 2026-05-23T19:42:11Z)
Source:     commit 8f548357 (clean), fingerprint sha256:abc123...
Build:      opt_level=2, sanitize=none, coverage=off
```

### C. `avra verify <binary> <source-tree>` 

Reproduce-and-compare:
1. Read build info from binary.
2. Check out source at the recorded commit (or use provided tree).
3. Build with the recorded flags.
4. Diff the binaries.
5. Report match / mismatch.

Pairs with reproducible builds (jg5z.4) to give a full "this binary came from this source" proof.

## Why this matters

- Debugging in production: "which version is this?" answerable from the binary alone.
- Supply chain: binary distributions can be verified against published source.
- Bug reports: "I'm running bs2 built from <fingerprint>" lets maintainers reproduce exactly.

## Acceptance

- Every bs2 binary contains a parseable `__avra_build_info` section.
- `avra info ./bin` extracts and prints it human-readable.
- `avra verify ./bin source-tree/` reproduces and compares.
- Implies (and is partially blocked by) jg5z.4 reproducibility work.

title: Benchmark regression tracking with statistical significance
description:
## Today

Performance changes are noticed ad-hoc ("the build feels slower"). No benchmark suite, no historical timing record. Selfhost cycle time is mentioned in CLAUDE.md as "~3 min" but that's gut memory, not a measurement someone is tracking.

## World-class equivalent

rustc-perf: runs a curated suite of benchmark programs on every commit. Charts wall-clock + instructions + memory over time. Bisects regressions automatically. Comments on PRs with "this PR regressed parser perf 8.3%."

Go's perflock + benchstat: per-bench statistical comparison ("is this within noise or a real change?").

Hyperfine: command-line statistical benchmarking with confidence intervals.

## Implementation for Avra

### A. Benchmark corpus

`benches/` directory with representative Avra programs:
- bench/parse_speed/   — large file, parser stress
- bench/typeck_heavy/  — generic-heavy code
- bench/codegen_large/ — many-fn module
- bench/selfhost/      — the bootstrap chain itself (bs2 compiles main.av)

Each bench has a known-good elapsed-time profile.

### B. `avra bench`

```
$ avra bench
Running 14 benchmarks (5 runs each, warmup 2)...
  parse_speed       42.3ms ± 1.2ms  (n=5)
  typeck_heavy     128.7ms ± 4.1ms  (n=5)
  codegen_large    312.4ms ± 8.9ms  (n=5)
  selfhost        2843ms  ± 47ms   (n=5)
  ...

Compared to baseline (commit b83c8444):
  parse_speed     ▼ 8.2% faster   (significant: p=0.003)
  typeck_heavy    ─ noise         (within ± 2σ of baseline)
  codegen_large   ▲ 3.1% slower   (NOT significant: p=0.12)
  selfhost        ─ noise

Baseline stored at .avra-bench-baseline.json. Update with: avra bench --update-baseline
```

Statistical engine: Mann-Whitney U test for "is this distribution different from baseline?" with p<0.05 threshold. Robust against the timing-jitter noise that plagues naive "did the wall-clock increase?" checks.

### C. CI integration

- PR pipeline runs `avra bench --compare-to=main` and posts results as PR comment.
- A significant regression (>5% on any bench with p<0.01) marks the PR for human review.
- Historical data in `bench-history/` (git-tracked or external dashboard).

## Why this matters

- Once jg5z.1 (daemon) lands, you NEED benchmarks to prove "yes this is actually faster."
- Perf regressions sneak in unnoticed without continuous measurement (Go ran into this repeatedly pre-perflock).
- Trustworthy benchmarks > marketing claims when evaluating Avra against alternatives.

## Acceptance

- `benches/` corpus with 10+ representative programs.
- `avra bench` runs the suite and reports statistically-significant deltas vs baseline.
- CI posts bench comparisons on PRs touching `bootstrap/`.
- Historical chart of selfhost timing over the last 90 days visible somewhere.

title: Property-based + fuzz testing framework
description:
## Today

Spec tests are example-based: `given "input X"; then "output Y"`. Excellent for documenting behavior, weak for finding edge cases. The 2405-test suite covers what the team THOUGHT to test. The lkze.9 work surfaced bugs that no test caught — they'd require generative inputs to find.

## World-class equivalent

QuickCheck (Haskell, original). Hypothesis (Python). proptest / quickcheck (Rust). Each generates random inputs against a property predicate; shrinks counterexamples to minimal form. Fuzzing: libFuzzer / AFL with sanitizer-instrumented binaries finds crashes nobody designed a test for.

## Implementation for Avra

### A. Spec-test extension: `forall`

Sister to `given`:

```avra
spec "vtype_eq is reflexive" {
    forall (t: ValueType) {
        then "t == t" { vtype_eq(t, t) }
    }
}
```

The runner generates N (default 100) random `ValueType` values. For each: if `then` returns false, shrink the input to minimal counterexample. Print it as part of the failure.

Generators auto-derived for:
- Primitives (int, string, bool, float)
- Enums (uniform variant pick, recurse into payload)
- Structs (each field generated independently)
- Lists (random length 0-32)
- Maps, Tuples, Options, Results

Manual `gen` overrides for tuning:

```avra
fn small_int_gen() -> Generator<int> { gen.int_range(0, 100) }

spec "list reverse is involutive" {
    forall (xs: List<int> gen=small_int_gen) {
        then "reverse(reverse(xs)) == xs" { ... }
    }
}
```

### B. Compiler fuzzer

`scripts/fuzz-compiler.sh` runs the bs2 binary against:
- Random valid Avra programs (grammar-fuzzer): should compile + run without crashing.
- Random INVALID Avra programs: should produce a diagnostic, never crash with F9999 (ICE).

Anything that crashes the compiler is a bug. Output: minimal repro saved to `tests/fuzz-corpus/`.

Integration with sanitizers (jg5z.5): run fuzzer against ASan-instrumented bs2; ASan reports = bugs.

### C. Continuous fuzzing in CI

Nightly fuzz job: 1 hour of fuzzing, archive any new crashes to GH issues automatically.

## Why this matters

- Property tests caught Avra-spec corner cases nobody designed tests for (e.g. the lkze.9 shape-coercion bug class would have surfaced as a property violation: "compiler IR for the same source must be byte-identical across edits that don't change semantics").
- Fuzzing the compiler is how you find ICEs (F9999) before users do. Rust ran fuzzers continuously for years; massive bug discovery.
- Self-hosted compiler + spec-driven language + decent test suite = the fuzzer is unusually high-leverage here.

## Acceptance

- `forall` syntax in the spec_test grammar.
- 5+ existing core invariants converted to `forall` properties (vtype_eq reflexive/symmetric/transitive, render_expr round-trips, etc.).
- `scripts/fuzz-compiler.sh` runs the grammar-fuzzer; first run finds at least one real bug (or proves the compiler is robust).
- CI nightly fuzz job wired in.

title: Build graph + critical-path visualization
description:
## Today

Per-phase timing JSON exists (`render_phase_timings` in cli/main.av — parse_ms, desugar_ms, resolve_ms, typeck_ms, mono_ms, codegen_ms). Good raw data, but no presentation. To answer "why is my build slow?" you'd squint at the JSON or grep logs.

## World-class equivalent

Bazel's `--profile=out.prof` + `bazel analyze-profile` shows critical-path nodes and per-action timing breakdowns. Cargo's `cargo build --timings` produces an interactive HTML chart showing per-crate parallel timeline + dependency arrows. ninja's `-d stats` dumps wallclock per command.

The signal that matters: **which 5 modules are bottlenecking the whole build, and what would I gain by speeding each one up?**

## Implementation for Avra

### A. `make build-graph` — static dep DAG

`avra build --emit-build-graph=build/graph.dot` writes a Graphviz DOT file:
- Nodes = packages or per-file (configurable)
- Edges = imports
- Node colour = recompile time
- Node size = output IR size

`make build-graph` runs that, then `dot -Tsvg` to render `build/graph.svg`. Trivial dev visual aid.

### B. `make build-profile` — runtime trace

`avra build --profile=build/profile.json` records per-phase per-module timings as a Chrome-tracing-format JSON. Drop into chrome://tracing or speedscope for an interactive flamegraph.

### C. `make build-critical-path` — bottleneck report

```
$ make build-critical-path
Total build: 8.7s wallclock, 14.2s CPU
Critical path (longest serial chain):
  1. parse @std/avrac           1.2s
  2. resolve_names @std/avrac   2.4s
  3. typeck @std/avrac          3.8s   ← biggest
  4. monomorphize cli           0.8s
  5. codegen cli                0.5s

Top single-fn cost in typeck:
  check_expr @std/avrac/typeck/mod.av     1.9s  (50% of typeck)
  resolve_use_names @std/avrac/resolve/   0.7s
  ...

Parallelism opportunity: 5.5s could become 2.1s with per-file incremental (jg5z.2)
```

## Why this matters

- Today, "the build is slow" is gut-feel. With data, you can prove which optimization is worth doing.
- After landing the daemon / incremental / distributed cache, this becomes the dashboard for measuring the wins.
- For library authors: see WHICH module's code is forcing rebuilds elsewhere (cache-miss attribution).

## Acceptance

- `make build-graph` produces an SVG of the package DAG.
- `make build-profile` produces a Chrome-tracing JSON viewable in speedscope.
- `make build-critical-path` prints a 1-page bottleneck report after each build.
- Phase timings (already collected) drive the report — just need presentation work.

title: First-class sanitizer build matrix (ASan/UBSan/TSan/MSan as profiles)
description:
## Today

`scripts/diagnose.sh --build-bs2-asan` exists (one-off ASan-instrumented bs2 build). UBSan / TSan / MSan: not wired in. Each sanitizer needs its own build flags, runtime hookup, and link line. Today these are ad-hoc shell incantations users would have to discover and assemble themselves.

## World-class equivalent

Rust: `cargo +nightly build -Z sanitizer=address` (or thread, leak, memory). Each sanitizer is a documented build mode with first-class CI integration. Go: `go test -race` for the race detector is universally taught. Clang/LLVM: `-fsanitize=address,undefined` composable, well-documented.

## Implementation for Avra

Make sanitizer builds first-class profiles in `avra build`:

```
avra build --sanitize=address     # ASan: use-after-free, heap-buffer-overflow
avra build --sanitize=thread      # TSan: data races (for spawn / parallel code)
avra build --sanitize=undefined   # UBSan: integer overflow, null deref, etc.
avra build --sanitize=memory      # MSan: uninitialized memory reads
avra build --sanitize=address,undefined  # composed
```

Each profile:
- Picks the right `-fsanitize=` linker flags.
- Links the corresponding sanitizer runtime.
- Disables incompatible optimizations.
- Sets `AVRA_SAN=<name>` env var so runtime can adapt (e.g. skip RC fastpaths that confuse ASan).
- Gets its own cache slot (sanitized builds shouldn't collide with normal builds in the cache).

Wire into `make test`:
- `make test-asan` — run full spec suite with ASan on (slow, ~5x).
- `make test-tsan` — same with TSan.
- Document in CLAUDE.md as the canonical 'I think I have a memory bug' checklist.

CI integration: nightly sanitized run flags any regression in heap-safety / race-freedom.

## Why this matters

- Avra is a self-hosted compiler with manual RC + arenas + threads. Heap correctness is load-bearing.
- TSan specifically: as spec Axis 18 (spawn / channels) matures, race bugs will be the dominant failure class.
- Catches the lkze.9-era 'silent shape coercion' class too — ASan would have screamed on the use-after-free that the obj-dump diagnostic eventually pinpointed.

## Acceptance

- `avra build --sanitize=address` produces a working sanitized bs2.
- Spec suite runs to completion under each sanitizer with zero warnings (modulo known false positives, documented).
- `make test-asan` / `make test-tsan` / `make test-ubsan` are Makefile targets.
- Nightly CI runs each; failures are visible.

title: Reproducible builds (deterministic IR + binary outputs)
description:
## Today

`make build` from the same source on different machines produces functionally-equivalent but not byte-identical binaries. The selfhost fixed-point check verifies bs2 ≡ bs3 from the same machine in the same session — but doesn't guarantee 'same machine tomorrow' or 'CI vs my laptop'.

Sources of non-determinism (likely):
- Embedded build timestamps
- HashMap iteration order if not deterministic
- Memory addresses leaking into mangled names (type registry uses ID counters — deterministic per-build but may vary if source-file-load order varies)
- Absolute file paths embedded in IR debug info or error strings (every `at=<src_file>:<line>` is an absolute path)
- Linker flags / library paths from system environment

## World-class equivalent

Reproducible Builds movement (reproducible-builds.org): same source → same bytes, on any machine, at any time. Required by Debian, NixOS, Bitcoin, security audits. Rust supports it via `--remap-path-prefix` + strip + sort-symbol-table flags. Go is reproducible by default since 1.10.

## Implementation for Avra

Audit + fix each non-determinism source:
1. Replace absolute file paths in IR/diagnostics with project-relative paths. Add `AVRA_REMAP_PATH=<prefix>` like Rust's `--remap-path-prefix`.
2. Sort symbol tables on emit (deterministic name ordering).
3. Use SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH env var for any embedded timestamps (the reproducible-builds.org standard).
4. Verify HashMap iteration is deterministic (or sort before emit).
5. Strip linker's machine-specific metadata (`-Wl,-no_uuid` on macOS, etc).

Add a regression check: `scripts/repro-check.sh` builds bs2 twice in different temp dirs with different mtimes, diffs the binaries, expects byte-identical.

## Why bother

- Supply chain: 'I can verify the binary on the package server came from the source I read.'
- Caching: deterministic outputs make distributed cache hits possible across users.
- Debugging: 'why did this change?' becomes provable from inputs.

## Acceptance

- Two `make build` invocations on different machines, same git SHA, same toolchain → byte-identical bs2 binary.
- `repro-check.sh` runs in CI; fails any non-deterministic regression.
- `avra build --reproducible` is the documented flag for users who want it.

title: Distributed/shared build cache (sccache-style team cache)
description:
## Today

Each developer's cache is isolated. Fresh checkout = cold build. CI never benefits from anyone else's work. New laptop = re-derive everything from scratch.

## World-class equivalent

sccache (Rust ecosystem, also works with C/C++): drop-in compiler wrapper that fetches/stores cache entries against a shared backend (S3, GCS, Redis, local NFS). Bazel's remote-cache: same idea, deeper integration. Nix: source code -> derivation hash -> binary substitute. Same shape regardless: content-addressed cache, optionally remote, with a clear hit-rate metric.

Result: clean checkout + cold build for a teammate is the same speed as a warm build for the person who last touched the code.

## Implementation for Avra

Build on the content-addressed cache from pdme (fp_full as the key). Add a backend abstraction:

```
trait CacheBackend {
    fn get(&self, fp: Fingerprint) -> Option<CacheEntry>
    fn put(&self, fp: Fingerprint, entry: CacheEntry) -> Result<()>
}
```

Implementations:
- LocalFsBackend (default — what pdme produces)
- S3Backend (`avra build --cache-backend=s3://bucket/prefix`)
- HttpBackend (`avra build --cache-backend=http://cache.team.dev`)
- ReadOnlyBackend (CI publishes; devs read-only — common security pattern)

Config via env var `AVRA_CACHE_BACKEND` or in a project `avra.toml`:

```toml
[cache]
backend = "s3://avra-cache.team.dev/v1"
mode = "read-write"  # or "read-only", "local-only"
```

## Security

- HMAC-signed entries (S3 bucket compromise can't poison everyone's build).
- Reject entries whose stored fp doesn't match the fetched-key fp (defence in depth on top of pdme.2).

## Acceptance

- CI publishes builds to shared cache; new developer's first build pulls cached artifacts → equivalent to warm rebuild.
- Hit rate observable via cache-stats (pdme.5).
- Local fallback when backend unreachable: builds still work, just cold.

title: Sub-package incremental compilation (per-file IR caching within a package)
description:
## Today

Cache granularity is the whole package. Edit one function in std-avrac/typeck/mod.av → invalidate the entire std-avrac cache → recompile every .av in std-avrac (hundreds of files). Even with pdme.1 landed, you'd still recompile too much.

## World-class equivalent

rustc's incremental compilation tracks dependency at the QUERY level — change one function, only re-typecheck/re-codegen the dependents of that function. Go's per-package cache is coarser but each package is much smaller. Swift's per-file .swiftinterface caching is the spiritual middle ground.

For Avra, the realistic target is per-file IR caching within a package:

- Cache key per file: `sha256(file source + transitive type signatures it imports)`.
- IR for each file stored separately in `packages/<pkg>/.cache/by-file/<file-fp>/unit.ll`.
- Final package IR assembled by concatenating live per-file IRs.
- File edit → only that file's fp changes → only that file recompiles → re-link.

## Why this matters

Today's flow: edit one fn in typeck/mod.av → 8-12 second rebuild. Target: 1-2 seconds. Compounds with #1 (daemon) — the daemon holds per-file IR in RAM and skips disk altogether for warm edits.

## Implementation

- Extend package_source_fingerprint logic to compute per-file fp alongside.
- Track per-file imports → typecheck-deps (the resolver already does this).
- Codegen output bucketed per-source-file (mostly already true — each .av becomes one ll subgraph).
- Linker step concatenates per-file IRs into the package's unit.ll.

## Risks

- Mono shared state (type registry, mangled names) needs careful handling — changes in file A might affect mangled names in file B that imports A's types.
- Conservative invalidation: when in doubt, invalidate. Worst case is too many recompiles, never wrong output.

## Acceptance

- Edit a one-function-body change in typeck/mod.av: rebuild touches only that file's IR.
- Total elapsed for trivial edit: <1.5s warm cache.
- Correctness: cache-fuzz (pdme.9) passes on every per-file edit.

title: Compiler daemon + watch mode (sub-second rebuilds)
description:
## Today's UX

Every `make build` / `avra check` is a cold process start: load LLVM, parse @std/*, build type registry, parse user source, … minimum ~2-3 seconds even for trivial edits. Devs notice and context-switch.

## World-class equivalent

`cargo check` after a small edit: <300ms. `rust-analyzer` keeps types live in editor with no perceptible lag. `gopls` has been sub-100ms on small projects for years.

The two pieces that get us there:

### A. Long-running compiler daemon

`avra daemon` starts a persistent process that:
- Parses + typechecks @std/* and the project once at startup.
- Holds the type registry, fingerprint cache, and LLVM context in RAM.
- Accepts requests via Unix socket: 'recompile file X', 'typecheck file X', 'emit IR for X'.
- Invalidates incrementally on source edits (subscribed via inotify/FSEvents).

Same architecture as rust-analyzer / gopls / sourcekit-lsp. We already have `avra lsp` — extend it to also serve build requests, or split a sibling daemon process.

### B. Watch mode

`avra watch [file]` runs the daemon and prints diagnostics + IR-size deltas every time a watched file changes:

```
[watch] packages/std-avrac/src/typeck/mod.av:1492 changed
[check] OK (137ms)  — 0 errors, 2 warnings
[build] IR size: 455_897 → 455_902 (+5 lines)
```

Or `avra watch --test` re-runs the spec suite for the affected modules.

## Implementation

- Reuse `avra lsp`'s parser + type-state machinery; add a non-LSP socket protocol for build commands.
- Filesystem notifier: `avra_fs_watch(paths)` extern wrapping inotify (Linux) / FSEvents (macOS) / kqueue (BSD).
- Incremental invalidation: when file X changes, dirty = transitive-revdeps(X); recompile only those.
- Editor integration through the existing LSP — the watch mode just makes the same machinery accessible to terminal-only users.

## Acceptance

- Cold start: equivalent to `make build` today (~2-3s).
- Warm edit-to-diagnostics: <300ms for typecheck-only.
- Warm edit-to-IR: <1s for a single-file change in a leaf package.
- Memory: <500MB resident for the bootstrap project size.
- Crash-safe: daemon crash falls back to cold-start, never corrupts cache.

title: World-class developer experience: daemon, distributed cache, reproducibility, error UX
description:
## Goal

Take Avra's build & dev workflow from 'correct and reasonably fast' to 'genuinely best-in-class — the thing developers cite when comparing compilers.' Not feature-creep. Each ticket here closes a gap between Avra today and what Rust / Go / Swift / Zig / Bazel users expect by default.

Filed alongside pdme (build cache correctness). pdme is what STOPS embarrassment; this epic is what BUILDS reputation.

## What separates 'fine' from 'world-class' build tools

The compilers people brag about share five properties:

1. **Sub-second feedback** during edit — daemon + watch + LSP-driven incremental
2. **Team-scale cache reuse** — distributed cache means cold-checkout build is fast for everyone
3. **Reproducible outputs** — same source → same bytes, anywhere, anytime. Supply-chain table stakes
4. **Diagnostic quality** — multi-span errors with suggestions; rustc set the bar, everyone copies it
5. **Observable internals** — when something's slow, you can SEE why (per-phase, per-module, per-fn timings; critical path)

Avra has the bones for most of this (LSP exists, per-phase timing exists, ASan exists). What's missing is the polish that turns scattered features into a coherent A-tier experience.

## Tickets

1. Compiler daemon + watch mode (sub-second rebuilds on save)
2. Sub-package incremental compilation (per-file IR caching within a package)
3. Distributed/shared build cache (sccache-style team cache)
4. Reproducible builds (deterministic IR + binary outputs)
5. First-class sanitizer build matrix (ASan/UBSan/TSan/MSan as built-in profiles)
6. Build graph + critical-path visualization
7. Error UX: Rust-grade multi-span annotations + 'did you mean' suggestions
8. Property-based + fuzz testing framework
9. Benchmark regression tracking with statistical significance
10. Source provenance embedded in binaries (commit + source hash for supply-chain)

## Out of scope

- Distributed REMOTE EXECUTION (Bazel-style remote-build cluster) — overkill for a single-language toolchain
- IDE plugin ports beyond LSP (the protocol is the API; downstream editors are not Avra's job)
- Package registry / dependency manager (separate epic — Avra has no external packages yet)
- Linker improvements / mold integration (system-level, not Avra-level)

## Sequencing recommendation

If you ever DO schedule this:
1. Start with #7 (error UX) — disproportionate user delight, low risk, no build-system surgery
2. Then #6 (visualization) — surfaces where #1/#2 will pay off most
3. Then #1 (daemon) — single biggest velocity win, but requires real engineering
4. Then #4 (reproducibility) — security/supply-chain value, mostly mechanical
5. Then the rest as prioritized

title: Cache-correctness fuzz test (regression net)
description:
## Problem

Cache correctness bugs are silent until they bite (lkze.9 spent 4+ hours on this exact failure mode). They never show up in any test because the test framework rebuilds before testing — masks the staleness. Need a dedicated regression test that EXERCISES the cache correctness invariant.

## Fix

`scripts/cache-fuzz.sh` that:

1. `make build` from cold (no caches). Capture full bs2 IR + test output as 'golden'.
2. For each `packages/<pkg>/src/**/*.av`:
   a. Add a no-op (a comment, or a dead let-binding) that changes file hash but not semantics.
   b. `make build`.
   c. `./build/bs2 compile packages/cli/src/main.av` → IR.
   d. Diff against golden. MUST equal (semantics unchanged → IR must be byte-identical to golden, modulo line-number debug info).
   e. `./build/bs2 test` → output. MUST match golden.
   f. Revert the file.
3. For each `packages/<pkg>/src/**/*.av`:
   a. Make a SEMANTIC change (rename a function, add an unused param). Compute the EXPECTED new IR by doing a full `make clean && make build`.
   b. `make build` (without clean). MUST equal the from-clean version.

Step 2 catches false-negative cache misses (re-compiled when it didn't need to — wasted work, not incorrect). Step 3 catches the real bug class (CACHE HIT served stale, IR diverges from what fresh-compile would produce). Step 3 is the lkze.9 repro.

Run nightly in CI; surface failures as red flags.

## Acceptance

- After landing pdme.1 + pdme.2 + pdme.8, fuzz passes for at least 100 random edit/rebuild cycles.
- The script is fast enough (under 30 min) to run as part of `make test-full` weekly.
- Documented as the canonical 'is the cache lying to me' check.

title: Include bs2 toolchain hash in cache fingerprint
description:
## Problem

The bs2 binary itself can change without source changing (e.g., a runtime.c edit triggers runtime.o rebuild, then bs2 relinks with new behaviour). The package cache currently doesn't see this — same source fingerprint, same cache hit, but the bs2 binary's codegen behaviour differs. Result: cache serves IR compiled by the OLD bs2 binary even though current bs2 would produce different output.

Concrete case from lkze.9 work: edited `runtime.c` (added diagnostic). bs2 binary rebuilt. But package caches kept serving the IR-version-compiled-by-previous-bs2. Behavior difference only surfaced after `make clean`.

There's already `read_or_compute_toolchain_fp` (test_runner/mod.av:401) used as part of test-fixture cache keys. The build-system cache should fold this in too.

## Fix

Compute `bs2_toolchain_fp = sha256(bs2 binary + runtime.o + llvm_wrapper.o)` once at build start. Fold into every package's fp_full from pdme.1.

```
fp_full(P) = sha256(
    fp_own(P)
    + transitive_dep_fps
    + bs2_toolchain_fp        # ← this ticket
    + profile_key
)
```

The toolchain fp is computed once at build start, cached in `build/.toolchain-fp` next to bs2. Recomputed only if any of bs2 / runtime.o / llvm_wrapper.o is newer than the sidecar.

## Files

- `build/fingerprint.av` — toolchain_fp() helper (or move from test_runner/mod.av)
- `build/driver.av` — fold into BuildInputs.compiler_hash (which already exists but is currently just bs2 mtime)

## Acceptance

- Edit `runtime.c` → `make build` invalidates every package cache and rebuilds.
- bs2 / bs3 / runtime untouched → caches hit, fast rebuild.
- The lkze.9-era 'I edited runtime.c and the build looked fine but behavior was stale' repro doesn't reproduce.

title: Concurrent-build cache lock (prevent parallel-compile corruption)
description:
## Problem

The bootstrap test runner spawns concurrent per-file test shards (`avra test`'s per-file mode). Each shard does its own seed-and-build sequence. If two shards race on the same package's cache:

- Shard A writes `packages/std-avrac/build/cache/<fp>/unit.ll` (in-progress)
- Shard B sees the entry exists, reads it, gets partial / zero-byte content
- Shard B errors with mysterious link-not-found / IR-parse errors

The existing `_tmp/<fp>.<pid>/` staging-then-rename pattern in cache.av:197 PARTIALLY handles this (concurrent reader sees either complete entry or none), but only for writes inside a single build invocation. Doesn't help when two whole bs2 processes race.

Symptoms today: occasional "shard X failed to compile/run" with link errors when running `make test` on a cold cache. Flake rate ~5% per CLAUDE.md hkms.3 work.

## Fix

Per-package file-lock using `flock(2)` (macOS / Linux). Build driver:

1. Before computing fingerprint or reading cache for package P, `flock(packages/P/build/cache/.lock, LOCK_SH)` (shared read).
2. Before writing, upgrade to `LOCK_EX` (exclusive write).
